reason: The key question is whether the comparison variable exists. Without this check a team could build a spurious comparison.
text: To test panel-vs-WES TMB correlation you need a WES-derived TMB (or WES mutation calls) for the same samples as the targeted-panel TMB. Before analysing, check whether such a variable exists: grep all clinical-table headers and '#' description lines for 'WES', 'exome', 'whole', and inspect data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and the mutation table's Center/Sequencer-type columns for any assay other than the MSK-IMPACT panels (IMPACT341/410/468). Do not construct a WES proxy from panel data; whether a genuine second assay is present decides whether the claim can be tested at all.

reason: Whether the exposure variable exists determines whether the claim can be tested at all, and using a proxy in its place would test a different hypothesis.
text: The hypothesis requires a community-level income exposure (e.g. census-tract or zip-level median income, area deprivation index) measured per patient. Before modelling, search every header and every '#' description line of all provided files for income, socioeconomic, deprivation, zip, tract, county, or other geographic identifiers. Do not substitute proxies such as race, smoking, PSA or disease extent for income. If an area-level income variable is present, model it with standard errors clustered by area (or a multilevel model), because patients from the same area are not independent.

reason: Whether a subtype-defining variable exists in the tables is the deciding question for which label the task rules allow; teams must check for it explicitly rather than infer subtype from genomic tables.
text: SCLC subtypes SCLC-A, SCLC-N and SCLC-P are defined by RNA or protein (IHC) expression of the transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3, not by any DNA mutation or copy-number change. Before choosing a label, list every file and column provided and search them (case-insensitive) for mRNA expression, IHC scores or a subtype annotation (ascl1, neurod, pou2f3, subtype). If such a variable exists, call subtypes per sample with a relative-expression rule (highest of the TFs) and report mixed ASCL1/NEUROD1 calls rather than forcing absence.

reason: Whether the measured variable exists at all decides which labels are possible. Teams need to check this first.
text: The hypothesis is about miRNA expression (miR-452, miR-766, miR-1180). The data are from a DNA-only targeted panel (MSK-IMPACT341): clinical, CNA, seg, gene panel and mutation files. Before any test, check every file for miRNA or RNA expression values (look for 'MIR'/'miR' rows and for any expression table), and check whether the panel gene list includes any MIR loci. Base the label on what you find.

reason: This is the central issue of the task: it decides whether the data can address the claim at all, and it stops activation from being read straight off a mutation list.
text: 'Pathway activation' is a functional claim, shown for example by phospho-ERK or MAPK transcriptional output. Before deciding, list every table and column provided (clinical, gene panel matrix, mutations MAF, SV) and check whether any expression, protein, phospho, pathway-score or functional-assay variable exists. If none does, finding ARAF N217I/G322S only shows that the mutations exist, not that they activate the pathway. Say explicitly which label the available variables can support and why.

reason: The claim has two parts, and one part may not be testable with these files. Teams need to check this before they let a proxy variable answer that part.
text: The hypothesis has two parts: KIT mutation enrichment AND focal amplification enrichment in Triple_WT. Check the provided tables (column headers of all files) for any copy-number, CNA, segment or GISTIC field. Focal amplifications need segmented copy-number data; they cannot be inferred from point-mutation calls, and ABSOLUTE ploidy is a whole-genome measure, not a focal amplification. Do not use ploidy or mutation counts as a stand-in. In your reasoning, say which part of the claim the data can test and which it cannot, and choose the label by applying the task's label definitions to that.

reason: Whether the hypothesis variable exists is the central question here. Teams could easily treat any TERT row in the MAF as a promoter mutation, or miss that the assay may never have targeted the promoter.
text: Recurrent TERT promoter mutations (C228T at chr5:1,295,228 and C250T at chr5:1,295,250, hg19) lie upstream of the coding sequence in a GC-rich region that whole-exome capture usually does not cover. Before testing anything, check whether this study records TERT promoter status at all: look for Hugo_Symbol == TERT rows in data_mutations.txt, read each row's Variant_Classification (5'Flank/5'UTR versus coding) and Start_Position, and search the clinical tables for any TERT-related column. A coding TERT variant such as a missense mutation is not a promoter mutation and should not be used in its place.

reason: This sets the logic of the decision. Teams often treat it as a frequency or exclusivity question and pick the wrong label.
text: The hypothesis is a universal negative: it claims no JAK2-nonmutated MPN patient carries a somatic CALR mutation. It is not a question about frequency, and the known near-mutual-exclusivity of CALR and JAK2 says nothing about whether it holds. Per sample, build JAK2 status and CALR status from data_mutations.txt (Tumor_Sample_Barcode joined to SAMPLE_ID), keep only MPN samples, and count samples that have a CALR mutation and no JAK2 mutation. One credible somatic CALR call in a JAK2-wild-type MPN sample is enough to refute the claim. A count of zero supports it only if those samples were actually profiled for CALR.

reason: This is the most likely trap: a high correlation between two panel-derived TMB columns could be mistaken for evidence about WES.
text: MUTATION_RATE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in data_clinical_sample.txt, and mutation counts recomputed from data_mutations.txt, all come from the same panel mutation calls (counts per panel Mb, with different filters or denominators). Correlating any of them with each other is circular and says nothing about panel-vs-WES concordance. To confirm, compute TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS/MUTATION_RATE per GENE_PANEL: a near-constant ratio shows they are rescalings of each other.

reason: Grouping by the clinical column or pooling unmatched samples would give the wrong comparison.
text: Lesion type is not a clinical column: CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED reads 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' for every sample, including JP and DCIS. Take lesion type from the SAMPLE_ID suffix (-JP, -DCIS, -IDC). Only patient JuP3 has a matched JP, DCIS and IDC. JuP1 and JuP2 have one unsuffixed sample each. The hypothesis is about JP versus its associated DCIS and IDC, so the main comparison is within JuP3 (JuP3-JP vs JuP3-DCIS vs JuP3-IDC). Do not pool the unmatched samples into a JP group, and state that one matched trio supports only a descriptive comparison.

reason: Whether the target population is present at all decides whether any ITH analysis is relevant to the claim. Teams have to check it first.
text: Before any heterogeneity analysis, confirm which cancers the cohort actually contains: tabulate CANCER_TYPE, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED and ONCOTREE_CODE in data_clinical_sample.txt, and grep every file for 'renal', 'kidney', 'CCRCC' and 'RCC'. The library's inspection found only colorectal, small bowel and unknown-primary cancers (an IBD/colitis-associated cohort, with no CCRCC code). Check this yourself. Heterogeneity seen in tumours of other types says nothing direct about clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and the hypothesis is about ccRCC only.

reason: This decides whether any test can be run at all. It also stops teams from reaching a True/False answer from ctDNA-versus-genomics associations that say nothing about anticoagulation or VTE.
text: Testing this hypothesis requires three things at patient level: a ctDNA-detected (yes/no) status, an anticoagulation exposure variable, and a VTE outcome (ideally with event timing). Before running any test, search every '#' description line and column header in data_clinical_patient.txt and data_clinical_sample.txt for terms such as VTE, thrombo, embol, DVT, PE, anticoag, LMWH, DOAC, heparin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, enoxaparin, warfarin, and for survival/follow-up columns. ctDNA status can be derived from plasma mutation/CNA/SV calls, but that alone does not make the claim testable. Do not use TMB, cancer type, mutation counts or other genomic features as stand-ins for VTE or anticoagulation. If the exposure or the outcome cannot be found, say so rather than building a proxy.

reason: The deciding question is whether any response variable exists at all; without checking, teams may call True or False from prior knowledge.
text: A claim about uniform versus heterogeneous in vivo chemotherapy sensitivity of engrafted tumoroids can only be tested with a per-model response variable, such as treated-versus-control tumour volume change, mRECIST class, growth curves, or IC50/AUC. Search every column and every '#' description line of all six files for terms like response, volume, growth, IC50, AUC, mouse, xenograft, engraft, mRECIST, treated or sensitivity, and name the exact column used. Whether the hypothesis sounds plausible clinically (rectal cancer response is known to vary) is not evidence either way; the label must rest on what the data columns actually contain.

reason: This stops the team from counting a race-only model as the race-plus-ancestry adjustment that the hypothesis specifies.
text: Self-reported RACE is a social category, not a measure of genetic ancestry. The hypothesis asks for adjustment for both race and ancestry, so look separately for a genetic-ancestry estimate (e.g. percent African/European ancestry, ancestry principal components). Do not report an ancestry adjustment when only RACE was used.

reason: Without this the comparator is easy to miss, which leads to a wrong 'Not verifiable' or to an analysis that never compares against established methods.
text: The established comparator is in the data. data_clinical_sample.txt has PROGNOSTIC_MODEL ('Genomic Risk Model Classification': Low/Medium/High), filled for roughly three quarters of samples. data_clinical_patient.txt has IPI (0-5), its five factor columns (IPI_AGE, IPI_LDH, IPI_ECOG, IPI_ANNARBOR_STAGE, IPI_EXTRANODAL_SITES) and OS_MONTHS/OS_STATUS. Count the patients who have PROGNOSTIC_MODEL, IPI and OS all present, and compare the genomic model with IPI head to head on them. Testing single genes against survival does not answer the question.

reason: The usual coding filter would silently delete exactly the variants the hypothesis is about.
text: Promoter mutations are non-coding and appear in a MAF only as 5'Flank (or sometimes 5'UTR/IGR/Intron) rows. Standard 'nonsynonymous only' filters (dropping Silent, Intron, UTR, Flank, IGR, RNA) remove them. Tabulate Variant_Classification for all NFKBIE rows BEFORE any filtering; this MAF contains 5'Flank and 5'UTR rows overall. Never conclude promoter mutations are absent from a coding-filtered table.

reason: Tells the team which kind of evidence the data can and cannot provide before they build an analysis around VAF.
text: Clonal selection means a shift in clone frequency (cellular prevalence), which normally needs allele read counts plus copy number and purity. The library reports that t_ref_count and t_alt_count in data_mutations.txt are empty for all rows; check this by counting non-empty values. If they are empty, do not claim that VAFs or prevalences rose or fell. Use what remains (mutations present in one sample and absent in another, and the copy-number tables) and say how much weaker that evidence is.

reason: Whether the data can test the central claim depends on this; it decides what analysis is even possible.
text: Chromoplexy (chains of interdependent translocations and deletions) is inferred from junction-level structural-variant calls that give both breakpoint coordinates and orientations for each junction (the input ChainFinder-type methods need). Before any chain analysis, list the columns of data_sv.txt and check whether both sites have chromosome, position and strand fields, and count rows per sample. If those fields are missing, chains cannot be reconstructed from this table; say the chain-inference variable is absent rather than building an ad hoc proxy and calling it chromoplexy.

reason: Exact string matching on the protein change can miss or misidentify the variants. Presence or absence alone is easily misread as support or contradiction.
text: Find the ARAF variants by checking Hugo_Symbol==ARAF in data_mutations.txt and ARAF in data_sv.txt. Inspect HGVSp_Short, Protein_position, Transcript_ID, Variant_Classification, genomic Start_Position/codon change and the carrying Tumor_Sample_Barcode. Protein positions depend on the transcript; the canonical ARAF transcript is ENST00000377045 / NM_001654. If the transcript is non-canonical, match on genomic coordinate or codon rather than the 'p.N217I' string. Finding the variants is not evidence for the hypothesis, and not finding them is not evidence against it.

reason: Without a measured normal group, a tumour-vs-normal comparison cannot be made. Teams could mistake germline-control barcodes for normal tissue profiles.
text: The claim compares tumours with normal liver. Count the sample groups in the clinical table (CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED / SAMPLE_CLASS; the library reports about 9 hepatocellular adenomas and 10 hepatocellular carcinomas). Check whether any normal-liver sample has its own measured profile. Matched-normal (_N) barcodes may be germline sequencing controls only, not a comparison group.

reason: Prevents misreading missing measurement as a negative result about subtype presence.
text: ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 may not be on the targeted sequencing panel used here; check whether they appear in data_cna.txt, the Hugo_Symbol column of data_mutations.txt and the panel in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt. A gene missing from these tables means it was not measured, not that the subtype is absent.

reason: Comparing unpaired pre and post frequencies mixes up acquired loss with tumours that were never amplified. Pairing defines what a selection event is.
text: Judge ERBB2 loss from within-patient pairs, not from unpaired groups. A post-trastuzumab sample without ERBB2 amplification shows acquired loss only if the same patient has a matched pre-treatment sample that is ERBB2-amplified. Pair samples by PATIENT_ID, using IMPACT_PRE_POST (PRE-TX / POST-TX) and sample-name suffixes (e.g. -P1/-P2/-M1a, -T01/-T02). Count the patients who are amplified pre-treatment and have a post-progression sample, then report how many of those pairs go from amplified to non-amplified.

reason: If teams re-derive subtypes or keep the NA samples in the comparison group, the enrichment result changes.
text: data_clinical_sample.txt already has subtype labels in MUTATION_TYPE (BRAF_Hotspot_Mutants ~150, RAS_Hotspot_Mutants ~92, NF1_Any_Mutants ~28, Triple_WT ~46, NA ~43). Use these labels instead of re-deriving subtypes. Drop NA samples from both groups. Test Triple_WT against all other labelled samples and also against each subtype separately. State which comparison group you used. KIT is reported as roughly mutually exclusive with BRAF/NRAS/NF1.

reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' label and clarifies what counts as contrary evidence.
text: data_cna_hg19.seg contains segmented copy number for JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC (and for JuP1 and JuP2), so CNA burden per lesion can be computed. The relevant variable therefore exists. If JP shows fewer or similar CNAs than its matched DCIS/IDC, that counts as evidence against the hypothesis, not as grounds for 'Not verifiable'.

reason: This defines the right unit of analysis. A pooled per-sample comparison answers a different question and could give the wrong label.
text: 'Acquiring new alterations' is a within-patient, over-time claim. Find patients with two or more samples (repeated PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt; use SAMPLE_TYPE such as Primary vs Recurrence/Metastasis, or sample suffixes T01/T02, to put them in order). For each patient, count alterations present in a later sample but absent from the earliest one. Then compare these per-patient acquired counts between fusion-negative (FN) and fusion-positive (FP) patients. Pooled per-sample alteration counts or TMB do not measure acquisition.

reason: Calling 8q gain with a naive log2 threshold ignores purity, ploidy and panel coverage, so the outcome would be misclassified.
text: Use the curated 8Q_ARM column in data_clinical_sample.txt as the 8q-gain outcome. If you recompute arm calls from data_cna_hg19.seg, use an arm-level rule (e.g. at least 70% of the arm covered by segments above about 0.2 log2), check agreement with the curated column, and prefer the curated column where they disagree.

reason: These choices decide whether a real correlation test is valid and read correctly, if such a test is possible.
text: If genuinely paired panel and WES TMB values exist: use Spearman, or Pearson on log(TMB+1), because TMB is right-skewed and hypermutators dominate raw Pearson. Keep one sample per patient. Normalise per panel-specific Mb or stratify by IMPACT panel version. Keep correlation separate from agreement: panels can show systematic bias (for example higher TMB) and still correlate highly, and the hypothesis is about correlation only.

reason: The hypothesis is restricted to MSS; the MSS definition and NA handling directly change the analysed cohort and can create spurious enrichment.
text: MSI-high colorectal tumours are mostly right-sided and carry BRAF V600E and RNF43 frameshifts (e.g. G659fs), so including them can make BRAF/RNF43 look right-enriched through MSI confounding alone. Tabulate MSI_STATUS (MSS/MSI/Inconclusive/NA) by PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION in data_clinical_sample.txt and analyse MSS only. Many samples (about 327) have MSI_STATUS=NA but an MSI_SCORE; decide explicitly how to handle them (e.g. MSIsensor cut-offs: <3 MSS, 3-10 indeterminate, >=10 MSI-H) and report results both for strict MSI_STATUS==MSS and for score-derived MSS.

reason: This defines what kind of evidence could support or refute a universal ITH claim. It also stops teams from reading single-sample or primary-vs-met data as proof of homogeneity or heterogeneity.
text: Spatial intratumor heterogeneity is measured by sequencing several regions of the same tumour. With a single biopsy, subclones are missed and mutations look clonal. Count samples per PATIENT_ID (the library saw 171 patients with 1 sample, 3 with 2 and 1 with 3), and use SAMPLE_TYPE to check whether repeat samples come from the same primary tumour or are primary/metastasis pairs. Primary-versus-metastasis differences reflect metastatic/temporal heterogeneity, not intratumor heterogeneity. Because the claim is universal ('all tumours'), refuting it would require a tumour shown to be homogeneous after adequate multi-region sampling. Not detecting subclones in one or a few samples is not evidence of homogeneity.

reason: Defines the right comparison unit. Mixing in later passages or xenograft-only patients would test a different claim.
text: The hypothesis is about INITIAL engraftment, meaning patient tumour (T) to the first xenograft passage. List the patients that have both a T sample and an early X sample (X0/X1 or the earliest available) on the same platform. Some patients (e.g. SA429, SA496) reportedly have xenograft samples only. Keep changes at later passages separate, because they answer a different question. Look for any variable that marks primary versus metastatic origin. If none exists, say so and judge the general claim on the pairs you have.

reason: This column is the most likely to be misread as drug-response data.
text: If data_clinical_sample.txt has a THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION (or similar) column, read its description line: it records the patient's treatment before the tumoroid was derived, not how the engrafted tumoroid responded in mice. It is a potential confounder of resistance, not a measure of sensitivity, unless a paired post-treatment outcome is also present.

reason: This sets the evidence standard for the label. Without it, a team could read a high raw mutation frequency as significance.
text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' is a statistical question. The percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not answer it, because large gene sets made of long genes get hit by chance. Count the samples with at least one nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare that count with a null model that accounts for each sample's mutation count and each gene's coding length (for example, permute each sample's mutations across genes weighted by CDS length, or run per-sample binomial tests and combine them PathScan-style). Make the call from the null-model p-value. A high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'.

reason: Whole-exome MAFs can contain germline or artefact calls that look like recurrent drivers.
text: For the ARAF rows, check dbSNP_RS, FILTER, t_alt_count/t_depth (VAF), and whether the same coordinate recurs across samples. Germline polymorphisms, low-VAF calls and duplicated records should not be counted as somatic activating events.

reason: This sets the criterion that decides the label. P-value comparisons are the most likely error.
text: To show 'outperforms', it is not enough for both predictors to be significant on log-rank, or for one to have a smaller p-value. Fit Cox models OS~IPI, OS~genomic model and OS~IPI+genomic model on the same patients. Compare discrimination (Harrell's C) and AIC, and run likelihood-ratio tests of the combined model against each single model. Outperformance means a clearly higher C for the genomic model, with a paired CI for the difference that excludes 0. Adding information beyond IPI (significant LRT) is a weaker claim and should be reported as such.

reason: A filter that keeps only SNVs or missense calls makes CALR mutations look absent, which biases the result toward the hypothesis.
text: CALR driver mutations are frameshift indels in exon 9. Type 1 is a 52-bp deletion (p.L367fs*46) and type 2 is a 5-bp TTGTC insertion (p.K385fs*47), and there are many rarer +1 frameshift variants. Exon 9 lies at about chr19:13054500-13055000 on GRCh37. For all Hugo_Symbol==CALR rows, tabulate Variant_Classification, Variant_Type and HGVSp. Do not filter to SNVs or missense calls, or to one protein change, because that misses these mutations. Count every exon 9 frameshift.

reason: Stops teams from using a weak genomic proxy as if it measured subtype.
text: MYC-family amplification (MYCL, MYC, MYCN) is only loosely associated with SCLC subtypes, and most SCLCs carry none, so CNA cannot assign or exclude a subtype for a sample. If tabulated, treat it as indirect context only, not as grounds for a True/False label.

reason: If the direct variable is missing, building a proxy is the most likely way to reach an unjustified conclusion.
text: TERT copy number, TERT expression itself, IDH1-wildtype status or ATRX-wildtype status are not measures of TERT promoter mutation. Expression is the outcome, so using it as a proxy is circular, and the IDH/ATRX links are only correlational. If no direct promoter-status variable exists, any proxy changes the hypothesis being tested and can be reported only as context, not as evidence.

reason: Matching on the gene symbol alone can miss promoter variants that VEP labelled with another gene.
text: Find NFKBIE variants by more than Hugo_Symbol. vcf2maf/VEP assigns each variant one gene, so a variant upstream of NFKBIE may carry a neighbouring gene's symbol; grep the all_effects column for NFKBIE. Entrez_Gene_Id is 0 throughout this MAF, and NFKBIE has the alias IKBE, so also match on SYMBOL, the Gene (ENSG) column, and a case-insensitive whole-line grep. Also select by genomic window: GRCh37 chr6, NFKBIE is on the minus strand, so its promoter lies at coordinates ABOVE the gene end (take gene coordinates from the MAF's own NFKBIE rows).

reason: Stops the team reading an incomplete SV table as negative evidence.
text: cBioPortal SV files often hold only curated fusions (e.g. ETS/ERG fusions), not the full somatic rearrangement catalogue. Compare the number of SV rows with the number of samples and tabulate Event_Info and genes. If the table is essentially a fusion annotation, a lack of chains or few rearrangements in it says nothing about whether rearrangements are rare or unchained.

reason: This sets the evidence standard for each label. Without it, a wide non-significant estimate can be misread as support for the claim.
text: The hypothesis is a null claim within a subgroup ('no benefit in ctDNA- patients'). A non-significant hazard ratio in a small ctDNA- group is absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect. Comparing p-values between subgroups is not a test of effect modification. If the variables exist, report the anticoagulation HR with its 95% CI in ctDNA- patients, give event counts, and run a formal ctDNA x anticoagulation interaction test. Support the claim only if the ctDNA- estimate is near null with a reasonably tight CI. If the CI still includes a meaningful benefit, describe the result as underpowered.

Before analysing, check whether such a variable exists: grep all clinical-table headers and '#' description lines for 'WES', 'exome', 'whole', and inspect data_gene

reason: This sets the population that the hypothesis is actually about. Including primary non-responders or samples taken before progression would dilute or distort any association.
text: Acquired trastuzumab resistance means the patient first benefited and then progressed on trastuzumab, with the post sample taken after progression. Restrict the analysis to patients whose treatment fields (e.g. TREATMENT, DETAILS_FIRST_LINE_COMMENTS) mention trastuzumab, who had HER2_RESPONSE CR/PR/SD, and who have a POST-TX sample. Confirm progression with HER2_TTP_ON_1ST_LINE_MONTHS and HER2_TX_STATUS. Exclude primary-refractory cases (best response POD) or analyse them separately, and state how many were excluded and why.

reason: Counting non-coding WGS calls inflates KIT frequencies in every subtype, and with a file this large the analysis needs to be run in chunks.
text: data_mutations.txt (274 MB, WGS) contains non-coding and silent variants (Intron, IGR, UTR, Flank, RNA, Silent). When counting KIT mutations, keep only non-silent coding classes: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift_Del/Ins, In_Frame_Del/Ins, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonstop. Count each sample at most once per gene. Read the file in chunks with usecols.

reason: The choice of CNA burden metric and noise filtering can decide the direction of the comparison.
text: Counting raw .seg rows measures segmentation, not alterations, and many segments may be copy-neutral. For each sample, compute (a) the number of segments, (b) the number of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold, and (c) the fraction of genome altered (bp with |seg.mean| > threshold divided by total bp). Also tabulate num.mark and segment length, and recount after excluding small or low-marker segments (e.g. num.mark<10 or <1 Mb). Base the conclusion on called alterations, and report it as metric-dependent if the metrics disagree on direction.

reason: Using CNA as a stand-in for expression is the most tempting wrong method on this data, and it would lead to a label the data cannot justify.
text: Copy number (gene-level CNA calls or seg.mean over the miRNA loci) predicts miRNA expression only weakly and unevenly. The IMPACT341 panel does not target these miRNA loci, so seg values there are interpolated from sparse probes. The groups are also tiny (about 9 vs 10), so a proxy test has little power, and running several tests can produce false positives. Do not treat a CNA-based proxy result as a test of expression.

reason: Duplicate samples inflate n and break the independence assumption.
text: Some patients have more than one sample (e.g. T01 and T02). Count SAMPLE_ID per PATIENT_ID, then keep one sample per patient or use patient-clustered models when relating patient-level variables to 8q status.

reason: Defines the correct population (metastatic) and the exposure variable (sidedness); both are easy to get wrong.
text: The hypothesis concerns metastatic CRC, but the cohort includes MCRC_TYPE='Early Stage Primary' samples (about 123) and about 14 samples with PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION=NA. Tabulate MCRC_TYPE and PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION; run the main analysis on mCRC samples (mCRC Primary + mCRC Metastasis) with known Left/Right side, and include early-stage samples only as a sensitivity analysis. Standard convention: right = caecum to transverse colon (proximal to splenic flexure), left = splenic flexure to rectum. Check PRIMARY_SITE against the provided Right/Left label; transverse colon handling varies and rectum may behave differently from left colon.

reason: Grouping by histology would put some patients in the wrong group, and that would change the FN vs FP comparison.
text: Define FP vs FN-RMS by whether a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusion is detected in data_sv.txt (Site1/Site2_Hugo_Symbol), in any sample of the patient, or by an explicit fusion-status clinical column if one exists. Do not define it by histology (ONCOTREE_CODE ARMS vs ERMS): about 20-25% of alveolar RMS are fusion-negative. Cross-tabulate fusion status against histology and report it.

reason: This stops teams from reading raw panel VAFs as evidence of subclonal structure.
text: The samples come from targeted panels (e.g. FoundationOne; see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt and GENE_PANEL), which give too few mutations per sample for reliable subclonal clustering, and different panels cover different genes. If you try to infer subclonality from VAF within a sample, correct for purity and local copy number (TUMOR_PURITY, coverage, t_alt_count/t_ref_count, CNA at the locus) to get cancer cell fractions. If purity or depth is missing or inadequate, treat ITH as not estimable rather than calling mutations subclonal from raw VAF.

reason: The data are mostly genomic, so teams may be tempted to use genomic diversity as a proxy for response.
text: Genomic heterogeneity between tumoroids (mutations, CNA, TMB) is not a measure of chemotherapy sensitivity; genotype-to-chemo-response links are weak. An argument built only from data_mutations, data_cna or TMB is indirect evidence about drug response and should not by itself be used to call the sensitivity claim supported or contradicted.

reason: This prevents a missense in a regulatory or kinase region from being inferred to be activating without a functional or downstream readout.
text: Background knowledge, not in the data: ARAF has low intrinsic kinase activity (non-canonical APE motif) and depends on dimerisation, so BRAF-hotspot logic does not carry over. Most ARAF missense variants have no functional characterisation; under AMP/ASCO/CAP and ClinGen/CGC/VICC rules, a novel kinase missense with no functional data is a variant of uncertain significance. Only a few ARAF variants have functional evidence, e.g. the S214 region and beta3-alphaC in-frame deletions. N217 lies near the CR2 S214 regulatory site and G322 near the start of the kinase domain; treat this domain proximity as suggestive only. Check whether any MAF annotation column (SIFT/PolyPhen, oncogenic flags) gives effect calls.

reason: Any analysis must be restricted to the model samples the hypothesis is about.
text: The cohort mixes PDX model samples and patient tumour samples (see SAMPLE_CLASS in data_clinical_sample.txt), and SAMPLE_TYPE values differ in case (e.g. Metastasis/metastasis). The hypothesis concerns PDX/CDX models only: filter by SAMPLE_CLASS and normalise case before counting anything.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Normal-cell contamination pulls segment log2 ratios toward 0. In a diploid genome, observed ratio = (purity*CN_tumour + (1-purity)*2)/2. A single-copy loss is -1.0 at 100% purity but log2(0.75) = -0.415 at 50% purity; a single-copy gain is +0.585 when pure. So low purity alone can produce low log2 amplitudes. Purity can be estimated without VAFs or BAFs from read depth alone: the log2 values of clonal CNAs cluster at levels set by purity (CNVkit docs approach 4; ABSOLUTE fits purity and ploidy to segmented copy number; AITAC uses read depth in deleted regions). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In copy-number analysis of tumour sequencing data, how does tumour cellularity (purity) attenuate segment log2 ratios, and what methods estimate purity from exome data when allele read counts are unavailable? ANSWER: Normal-cell contamination pulls observed copy ratios toward 1 (log2 toward 0). For a diploid genome, observed ratio = (p*CN_tumour + (1-p)*2)/2. A single-copy loss is log2(1/2) = -1.0 when pure but log2(0.75) = -0.415 at 50% purity; a single-copy gain is +0.585 when pure and smaller as purity falls. So low purity alone can explain low log2 amplitudes, and amplitude alone cannot tell low purity apart from subclonality or genuinely few or small CNAs. Without VAFs or BAFs, purity can be estimated from read depth only: (a) the log2 values of clonal CNAs cluster at levels set by purity and ploidy (CNVkit docs approach 4; ABSOLUTE fits purity and ploidy from segmented copy number plus karyotype priors); (b) AITAC estimates purity from read depths in deleted regions alone; (c) a pathologist's cellularity estimate. Fits from copy number alone are ambiguous between purity and ploidy and less reliable than allele-based methods. Sequenza, PurityEst, PurBayes, TPES and THetA2 (BAF mode) need allele or SNV data. A rough check with no allele data: if a lesion's strongest clonal-looking losses sit near -0.4 rather than -1, that fits about 50% purity. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/heterogeneity.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7205152/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer-genomics papers, when a lesion is said to show a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as the count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered? ANSWER: The web does not settle a single convention. The CINmetrics comparison of six burden metrics (TAI, modified TAI, CNA count, breakpoints, altered base segments, FGA) across TCGA found that they do not always agree and warns against treating them as interchangeable. The wording 'number of CNAs' literally implies a count of events or segments. Since the source paper's metric is unknown, the robust approach is to compute both and report whether they agree. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/SqtGhn-AZ4s, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10245901/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In exome or targeted sequencing studies of myeloproliferative neoplasms, how is JAK2 V617F status usually determined (for example, allele-specific PCR versus sequencing calls), and how often do low-allele-burden JAK2 V617F cases go undetected by exome variant calling? ANSWER: JAK2 V617F is usually typed by allele-specific quantitative PCR on granulocyte DNA, the most common lab method. In the landmark exome studies (Klampfl 2013; Rumi 2014), JAK2 status came from this separate assay, not from exome calls. Sequencing is less sensitive. In Maslah 2019 (427 patients), the NGS detection limit was about 2% VAF. NGS missed 21 samples that qPCR measured at 0.1-1% burden, plus 1 of 298 at 3%. Concordance was excellent above 2%. Lower-depth exome calling will miss at least as many low-burden cases. I found no figure specific to exome calling. 'No JAK2 call in the MAF' is therefore only a weak proxy for JAK2-nonmutated. A study-provided JAK2 genotype or clinical column should take precedence when one exists. HOW SURE: high for the method and NGS sensitivity limits; medium for how this carries over to exome calling. text: FINDING: True loss of ERBB2/HER2 amplification at progression is distinguished from low purity/heterogeneity by (a) requiring adequate tumor purity before trusting a non-amplified NGS call (hybrid-capture NGS such as MSK-IMPACT becomes unreliable for low-level amplification when purity <50%, and discordances with IHC/FISH occur specifically in low tumor content and HER2 heterogeneity), (b) purity-corrected copy-number/log2 fold-change falling below the amplification cutoff rather than relying on raw copy number, and (c) orthogonal confirmation by ASCO/CAP FISH (HER2/CEP17 ratio >=2.0 or >=6 copies) and IHC; mosaic intratumoral heterogeneity is conventionally defined when 5-50% of scored cells are amplified. A non-amplified post-treatment call from a low-purity sample is not accepted as true loss. QUESTION: How is loss of HER2 amplification at progression distinguished from sampling heterogeneity or low tumor purity, and what thresholds are used? text: FINDING: Acquired (secondary) trastuzumab resistance is conventionally defined as disease progression AFTER an initial period of clinical benefit on a trastuzumab-containing regimen, in contrast to primary/de novo resistance (progression at the first radiological reassessment, ~8-12 weeks or within 3 months of starting first-line trastuzumab, or recurrence during/within 12 months of adjuvant trastuzumab). The Wong et al. unifying definition further defines trastuzumab-REFRACTORY disease as progression after two or more trastuzumab-containing regimens that each initially achieved objective response or stable disease at first assessment. Clinical-genomics studies typically require a documented best response of objective response or stable disease (commonly a minimum clinical benefit of ~6 months) before progression, with the post-progression biopsy taken at the time of progression on therapy. Differing eligibility (e.g., 20 vs 22 pairs) usually reflects differing minimum-benefit/response thresholds applied to this definition. QUESTION: How is acquired trastuzumab resistance conventionally defined (best response, minimum duration of benefit, biopsy timing)? SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1634/theoncologist.2011-0165

text: FINDING: To claim selection of a PRE-EXISTING subclone lacking a driver amplification (rather than de novo amplification loss), genomic studies conventionally require positive evidence that the non-amplified population existed before treatment: detection of the non-amplified/alternative clone in the pre-treatment sample via sensitive methods (deep targeted sequencing, single-cell/multiregion sampling, or ctDNA), and phylogenetic/clonality reconstruction (cancer cell fraction analysis) showing the resistant lineage branched off before therapy and then expanded under selection. Branching of a phylogenetic tree alone does NOT imply selection, because branching is the natural product of neutral mutational processes; a formal signal of positive/subclonal selection (e.g., dN/dS, subclonal selection modelling) is needed. The classic paradigm is pre-existence and clonal selection of MET amplification in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. De novo loss would show no detectable pre-existing non-amplified population and no ancestral branch predating treatment. Sensitivity to detect a minor pre-existing subclone is limited by sampling breadth and sequencing depth, so absence of detection is not proof of de novo origin. QUESTION: What evidence is required to claim clonal selection of a pre-existing subclone lacking a driver amplification vs de novo amplification loss? SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41576-019-0114-6 ; https://doi.org/10.1634/theoncologist.2011-0165

text: FINDING: BRAF class 1 (V600E), class 2 (e.g. codons 469/597/601) and class 3 (kinase-impaired, codons 466/594/596) are all treated as pathogenic drivers. V600E is strongly right-sided and MSI-associated. Non-V600 class 2/3 mutations are linked to microsatellite stability and distal (left) location; class 3 is significantly more left-sided than class 1 (Schirripa 2019, P=0.0028) and often co-occurs with RAS mutations. A Tempus study (n=3,391) found no significant difference in KRAS variant-type distribution between left and right colon, though overall KRAS mutation was higher on the right (52% vs 43%). A smaller study (n=722) found G12D, G12V and G13D associated with right-sided tumours. There is no strong evidence that KRAS subclasses have opposite side distributions. QUESTION: When comparing two prognostic scores with different numbers of levels (e.g. a 3-group classifier vs a 6-level ordinal index) for survival, what is the accepted way to establish that one 'outperforms' the other: difference in Harrell's/Uno's C with a paired CI, likelihood/AIC, net reclassification, or decision-curve analysis? Is collapsing the finer score to fewer groups considered a fair comparison? ANSWER: No single mandated metric. Methodologists favour likelihood-based comparison: an LR chi-square test for nested models (does the new score add information to the IPI in a Cox model, and the reverse), and AIC/BIC for non-nested models. A difference between two C-indices is rank-based and has low power; if C is used, Harrell recommends a paired head-to-head comparison (Hmisc rcorrp.cens) over two separate Cs. Categorical NRI depends on arbitrary cut points and is discouraged. Decision curves measure clinical net benefit, not discrimination. Collapsing the finer comparator to fewer groups throws away information and lowers the bar for the new score, so it is not a fair comparison. DLBCL practice (Ruppert et al., Blood 2020) compared IPI, R-IPI and NCCN-IPI each in its standard grouping by C-index. It also used a nested test: NCCN-IPI categories stayed prognostic within each IPI group, but not the reverse. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.fharrell.com/post/addvalue/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6460632/, https://doi.org/10.1182/blood.2019002729.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In paired pre- and post-treatment biopsy studies of HER2-amplified solid tumours, how is 'loss of HER2 amplification' at progression distinguished from sampling heterogeneity or low tumour purity, and what thresholds or criteria are conventionally used? ANSWER: True loss is accepted only when a non-amplified call is not explained by low tumor purity. Hybrid-capture NGS (e.g. MSK-IMPACT) becomes unreliable for low-level amplification when tumor purity is below ~50%, and discordances with IHC/FISH occur specifically in low tumor content and HER2 heterogeneity, so a non-amplified post-treatment call from a low-purity sample is not counted as loss. Conventionally one requires adequate purity, purity-corrected copy-number/log2 fold-change falling below the amplification cutoff (rather than raw copy number), and orthogonal confirmation by IHC and ASCO/CAP FISH criteria (HER2/CEP17 ratio >=2.0 or >=6 HER2 copies). Intratumoral (mosaic) heterogeneity is conventionally defined when 5-50% of scored cells are amplified, which is the main confounder to exclude. There is no single universally fixed numeric NGS threshold; the key safeguards are a purity floor and orthogonal/method-corrected confirmation. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5397722/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9771738/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is 'acquired' trastuzumab resistance conventionally defined in clinical genomics studies (required best response, minimum duration of benefit, timing of the post-progression biopsy)? ANSWER: Acquired (secondary) resistance is progression after an initial period of clinical benefit on a trastuzumab-containing regimen, as opposed to primary/de novo resistance (progression at the first radiological reassessment, ~8-12 weeks or within 3 months of starting first-line trastuzumab, or recurrence during/within 12 months of adjuvant trastuzumab). The Wong et al. unifying definition additionally defines trastuzumab-refractory disease as progression after >=2 trastuzumab-containing regimens that each first achieved objective response or stable disease. In practice clinical-genomics studies require a documented best response of objective response or stable disease (often a minimum clinical benefit on the order of ~6 months) before progression, with the post-progression biopsy taken at progression on therapy. Differing minimum-benefit/response thresholds applied to this definition explain differing eligible pair counts (e.g. 20 vs 22). HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1634/theoncologist.2011-0165.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What evidence do genomic studies conventionally require to claim clonal selection of a pre-existing subclone lacking a driver amplification, as opposed to amplification loss arising de novo? ANSWER: To claim selection of a pre-existing non-amplified subclone, studies require positive evidence that the non-amplified population existed before treatment: detection of that clone in the pre-treatment sample using sensitive methods (deep targeted sequencing, single-cell or multiregion sampling, or ctDNA), plus phylogenetic/clonality reconstruction (cancer cell fraction analysis) showing the resistant lineage branched off before therapy and then expanded under selection. A formal signal of positive/subclonal selection (e.g. dN/dS or subclonal-selection modelling) is expected, because branching of a phylogenetic tree alone does not imply selection — branching is the natural product of neutral mutational processes. The canonical example is pre-existence and clonal selection of MET amplification in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. De novo loss instead shows no detectable pre-existing non-amplified population and no ancestral branch predating treatment; however, because sensitivity to detect a minor pre-existing subclone is limited by sampling breadth and sequencing depth, failure to detect it does not by itself prove de novo origin. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41576-019-0114-6, https://doi.org/10.1634/theoncologist.2011-0165.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Standard pathway-level mutation tests use a background-mutation-rate null that accounts for gene length and, in most cases, sample-specific mutation burden. PathScan (Wendl et al. 2011) computes for each sample the probability of the observed number of mutated pathway genes under a random-mutation null at background rate rho, with each gene's hit probability set by its length; it then combines the per-sample p-values by Fisher-Lancaster. MutSig/MutSigCV scores mutations against a patient-specific background rate mu_p over covered bases per gene, with gene-specific covariates. Weighted-resampling methods (Jia & Zhao 2012) build gene weights from individual BMR x gene length. Naive hypergeometric tests that weight all genes equally are described as biased toward long-gene pathways. So a length-aware and burden-aware null is the standard. QUESTION: How do standard pathway mutation significance methods define the background model re gene length and per-sample burden? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356304/ ; https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/ ; https://gdac.broadinstitute.org/runs/analyses__2014_01_15/reports/cancer/CESC-TP/MutSigNozzleReportMerged/nozzle.html

text: FINDING: Published PDX studies use a few criteria to call selection rather than drift or sampling. (a) Reproducibility: the same clonal expansion or CNA shift appears in independent replicate grafts of the same tumour (Eirew et al. 2015 Nature, 'clonal dynamics are reproduced in replicate transplants'). (b) A minor clone (<5% of the starting population) becomes dominant on engraftment, i.e. a subclonal-to-clonal transition (Eirew 2015; Ben-David 2017). (c) Recurrence of the same changes in PDXs from the same primary tumour (Ben-David 2019 review) or enrichment of cancer genes in PDX-specific CNAs across models (Woo 2021 found no enrichment). (d) Comparing patient-vs-PDX CNA differences with multiregion variation within the same patient as a null for spatial sampling (Woo 2021 found the two comparable). A difference above technical noise alone is not treated as evidence of selection. QUESTION: Criteria for separating clonal selection from drift or spatial sampling using CN segments alone. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature13952 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493335/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Tumour-only (unmatched) calling cannot remove private germline variants. Database filtering (dbSNP, 1000G, ESP, ExAC) removes only common polymorphisms. Jones et al. 2015 (815 tumour-normal pairs) found that after removing common germline variants, tumour-only analysis still gave false positives making up 31% of alterations in targeted panels and 65% in exomes (about 249 of 382 candidate calls per exome were germline). The rate is higher in non-European individuals because population databases are less complete for them (BMC Med Genomics 2017). A matched normal removes these variants. So variants seen in an unmatched tumour but absent in a matched-called derived sample may be residual germline variants rather than real mutation loss. QUESTION: Tumour-only vs matched calling and residual germline fraction after dbSNP filtering. SOURCE: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4442685/ ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12920-017-0296-8 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561496/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The observed log2 copy ratio depends nonlinearly on purity p and ploidy. CNVkit docs say the copy ratio depends on purity, ploidy and subclone size; in a pure diploid sample a one-copy gain is log2(3/2)=0.585 and a one-copy loss is -1. The standard admixture model (ASCAT/ABSOLUTE; I did not see the equation itself in the text I fetched) is log2R = log2[(p*CN + 2(1-p)) / (p*ploidy + 2(1-p))]. Linear in the ratio space 2^log2R, it is nonlinear in log2 and compresses losses more than gains. So rescaling one sample's log2 ratios linearly against another's cannot fully remove a purity difference, especially for deep losses and high-level gains. The ploidy recentring term also shifts the baseline. Converting to absolute copy number, or working in ratio space and using 2^x, is the appropriate correction. QUESTION: Dependence of log2 ratio on purity and ploidy; adequacy of linear regression. SOURCE: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383288/ ; https://unclineberger.org/peroulab/wp-content/uploads/sites/1008/2019/06/Aug-23-ASCAT-aCGH-VanLoo-PNAS-2010.pdf

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In standard practice the universe is the sequenced territory: all genes on the exome/target, weighted by their (covered) coding length. MutSig counts covered bases per gene and patient, and PathScan uses gene lengths under a genome/exome-wide BMR. The pages I read never use a universe of only the genes observed mutated. Restricting to mutated genes conditions on the outcome and drops the many unmutated genes, which removes the length and burden information the null needs. The web pages I read do not quantify the size of this bias, so the bias direction is my reasoning, not something a source states. QUESTION: Which gene universe is conventional in gene-set tests on somatic mutations, and how does the choice bias results? SOURCE: https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/ ; https://gdac.broadinstitute.org/runs/analyses__2014_01_15/reports/cancer/CESC-TP/MutSigNozzleReportMerged/nozzle.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356304/

text: FINDING: The answer depends on the definition. In KEGG ErbB signaling (MSigDB KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY, 87 genes), KRAS, NRAS and HRAS are members, along with EGFR, ERBB2-4, PIK3CA/PIK3R*, AKT1-3 and MTOR. QUESTION: Are KRAS/NRAS counted in an ERBB-PI3K pathway or a separate RTK-RAS pathway? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer genomics studies, how is primary tumour sidedness conventionally defined (placement of transverse colon, splenic flexure and rectum)? Are rectal tumours usually analysed separately from left colon tumours when comparing mutation frequencies by side? ANSWER: The most common convention splits at the splenic flexure. Right-sided means caecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure and the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon (midgut). Left-sided means the splenic flexure (and distal third of the transverse colon), descending colon, sigmoid and rectum (hindgut). There is no single agreed definition. Because the transverse colon has a mixed embryological origin, some studies exclude it, and rectal cancer is often excluded or reported as a third group (e.g. Caris: right colon, left colon, rectum). Many mCRC studies do include rectum in the left group, since metastatic treatment is the same. Mutation rates vary along a continuum. Loree et al. found that the sigmoid-rectal region has fewer PIK3CA, BRAF and CTNNB1 mutations and less MSI than other left-sided sites, and that transverse tumours cluster closer to left-sided ones. The choice of definition can therefore move per-gene results, so a sensitivity analysis (colon-only, transverse excluded) is advisable. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.6004/jnccn.2017.0038, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/24/5/1062/81237/Classifying-Colorectal-Cancer-by-Tumor-Location, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5689690/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7505124/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which BRAF and KRAS variant classes (e.g. BRAF class 1 V600 vs class 2/3 non-V600; KRAS codon 12/13 vs Q61/A146/K117) are considered oncogenic, and do they differ in their distribution between proximal and distal colorectal tumours? ANSWER: BRAF: class 1 (V600E), class 2 (codons 469/597/601, active dimers) and class 3 (kinase-impaired, codons 466/594/596, RAS-dependent) are all treated as pathogenic drivers. Their side distributions run in opposite directions. V600E is proximal (right-sided) and MSI-associated. Non-V600 class 2/3 mutations are associated with microsatellite stability and distal location: class 3 is significantly more left-sided than class 1 (P=0.0028), class 2 looks like class 1, and class 2/3 often co-occur with atypical RAS mutations. Counting class 2/3 as oncogenic under one gene-level BRAF rule would therefore dilute right-sided enrichment; this is most relevant in MSS tumours, where non-V600 mutations make up a larger share. KRAS: hotspots at G12, G13, Q61, K117 and A146 are all considered activating. A large Tempus cohort (n=3,391) found no significant difference in KRAS variant-type distribution between left and right colon, although overall KRAS mutation was more frequent on the right (52% vs 43%). A smaller cohort (n=722) found G12D, G12V and G13D associated with right-sided tumours. G13D is more MSI-associated. I found no strong evidence that KRAS subclasses run in opposite side directions. I did not read a source specifically on A146/K117 sidedness. HOW SURE: medium (high for BRAF classes, medium for KRAS subclasses). SOURCES: https://aacrjournals.org/mcr/article/23/4/300/754233/Coevolution-of-Atypical-BRAF-and-KRAS-Mutations-in, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/25/13/3954/81843/Class-1-2-and-3-BRAF-Mutated-Metastatic-Colorectal, https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2023.41.4_suppl.231, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11763696/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-11530-0.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which RNF43 alterations (e.g. G659fs and other truncating variants) are considered oncogenic driver events rather than passenger or MSI-associated events in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer? ANSWER: RNF43 truncating mutations are strongly enriched in MSI-H CRC. Two recurrent frameshift hotspots, G659fs (about 48% of RNF43 mutations in a TCGA re-analysis, about 8% of CRC) and R117fs, sit at mononucleotide repeats that are prone to MSI slippage. Whether G659fs is functional is disputed. Earlier work found that the G659fs protein still degrades Frizzled and does not make tumours Wnt-dependent; an organoid carrying it did not respond to PORCN inhibitors, and such patients were excluded from PORCN inhibitor trials. Fang et al. (Nat Commun 2022) report a Wnt-independent oncogenic role through PI3K/p85. Seeber et al. (CCR 2022) report that about 99% of G659fs cases were MSI-H/TMB-high; I took this from the abstract/snippet and did not read the full text. In MSS CRC, RNF43 mutations occur mainly in the BRAF V600E/serrated pathway (26% of pMMR/MSS BRAF V600E mCRC), which is itself right-sided. Practical takeaway: in MSS tumours, G659fs/R117fs calls should be checked as possible MSI-like or artefact events, and non-hotspot truncating mutations (nonsense or frameshifts outside the homopolymer hotspots) plus clearly inactivating alterations are the more defensible driver set. The web did not give a definitive MSS-specific driver list; OncoKB annotations were not consulted. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-30794-7, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4283570/, https://doi.org/10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-21-3018, https://gut.bmj.com/content/66/9/1645.full, https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.23.00255.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How do standard pathway-level mutation significance methods (e.g. PathScan, MutSig-style gene-set tests, Hotnet-type approaches) define the background model, and specifically how do they account for gene coding length and per-sample mutation burden? ANSWER: They use a background-mutation-rate (BMR) null that accounts for gene length and usually for each sample's mutation burden. PathScan tests each sample separately: it computes the probability of the observed number of mutated pathway genes under random mutation at background rate rho, with each gene's hit probability set by its length. It then combines the per-sample p-values by Fisher-Lancaster. MutSig/MutSigCV scores mutations against a patient-specific background rate over each gene's covered bases, with gene-specific covariates (expression, replication time). Weighted-resampling pathway methods (Jia & Zhao 2012) weight each gene by the individual's BMR times gene length. Naive hypergeometric tests that treat all genes equally are described as biased toward pathways of long genes. So the standard is a null that accounts for both length and burden. I did not read a HotNet source, so this answer does not cover HotNet-type methods. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356304/, https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://gdac.broadinstitute.org/runs/analyses__2014_01_15/reports/cancer/CESC-TP/MutSigNozzleReportMerged/nozzle.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In gene-set permutation tests on somatic mutation data, what gene universe is conventionally used (all genes in the exome, genes on the sequencing target, or only genes observed mutated), and how does the choice bias the result? ANSWER: The convention is the sequenced territory: all genes in the exome or on the capture target, weighted by their covered coding length. MutSig tabulates covered bases per gene and patient, and PathScan uses gene lengths under an exome-wide BMR. None of the sources I read use a universe of only the genes observed mutated. My reasoning, not stated by any source: restricting to mutated genes conditions on the outcome and discards the length and burden information the null needs, so results from it are not comparable to standard tests. A whole-exome or target universe with length weighting is the defensible version. The pages I read do not settle exactly how large or in which direction the bias is. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://gdac.broadinstitute.org/runs/analyses__2014_01_15/reports/cancer/CESC-TP/MutSigNozzleReportMerged/nozzle.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3356304/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In commonly used cancer pathway definitions (e.g. TCGA pan-cancer oncogenic signaling pathways, KEGG ErbB), are RAS genes such as KRAS and NRAS counted as part of an 'ERBB-PI3K' pathway or as a separate RTK-RAS pathway? ANSWER: It depends on the definition. KEGG ErbB signaling (MSigDB KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY, 87 genes) includes KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, along with EGFR, ERBB2-4, the PIK3 subunits, AKT1-3 and MTOR. TCGA pan-cancer (Sanchez-Vega et al., Cell 2018) puts KRAS, NRAS and HRAS in the RTK-RAS pathway together with the ERBB receptors, and treats PI3K/Akt as a separate pathway. It has no combined 'ERBB-PI3K' pathway. An ERBB-PI3K set based on KEGG ErbB would therefore include RAS genes, and a TCGA-style set would not. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/human/geneset/KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY.html, https://www.cell.com/article/S0092867418303593/pdf, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29625050/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In MAFs annotated with Oncotator, what do the TCGAscape_Amplification_Peaks and Tumorscape_Amplification_Peaks fields contain: a sample-specific copy-number call, or a gene-level annotation taken from a pan-cancer GISTIC peak list? ANSWER: Gene-level annotation, not a sample-specific call. Oncotator describes its annotations as variant- and gene-centric, drawn from pooled public resources. MAF headers list these sources as fixed, versioned datasets: 'TUMORScape 20100104' and 'TCGAScape 110405'. Tumorscape is the Broad portal of the Beroukhim et al. 2010 (Nature) GISTIC analysis of 3,131 cancers. It reports the most significant amplification and deletion peak regions for each cancer type and the copy-number significance of each gene. TCGA Tumorscape is the same kind of analysis for about 11,000 TCGA cancers. These fields therefore record which published pan-cancer recurrent amplification peaks (by cancer type) contain the mutated gene. They are identical for every sample with a mutation in that gene and say nothing about that tumour's own copy number, so they cannot test sample-level focal amplification. Caveat: none of the pages I read gives a formal column definition; this is inferred from the datasource versions and the portal descriptions. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52021940/concatenate-two-dataframes-and-write-back-to-xlsx-file, https://web.archive.org/web/20120414021752/http:/www.broadinstitute.org/tumorscape/pages/portalHome.jsf, https://beroukhimlab.org/data-and-tools/, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/humu.22771.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In tumour-vs-derived-sample comparisons without allele read counts, what criteria do published methods use to separate clonal selection from neutral drift or spatial sampling differences, using copy-number segment data alone (e.g. recurrence across cases, subclonal-to-clonal transitions)? ANSWER: Published PDX work uses: (a) reproducibility, meaning the same clonal or CNA shift appears in independent replicate grafts of the same tumour, which argues against random drift (Eirew 2015, 'clonal dynamics are reproduced in replicate transplants'); (b) a minor subclone (<5% of the starting cells) expanding to dominance, i.e. a subclonal-to-clonal transition such as an intermediate-level segment becoming clonal (Eirew 2015; Ben-David 2017, 'selection of pre-existing minor clones'); (c) recurrence of the same changes across independent PDXs from one tumour (Ben-David 2019 review: 'indicating the involvement of selection, rather than mere genetic drift') or enrichment of cancer genes in PDX-specific CNAs across models (Woo 2021 found none); (d) a sampling null, comparing patient-vs-PDX CNA differences with multiregion variation within the same patient (Woo 2021 found them comparable, which argues against systematic selection). A difference above technical noise alone is not accepted as evidence of selection. These methods are qualitative and comparative; I found no formal CN-only statistical test separating selection from drift. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature13952, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5659952/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493335/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How do somatic variant callers run in tumour-only (unmatched) mode differ from matched tumour-normal mode in retaining private germline variants, and how large is the typical residual germline fraction after dbSNP filtering? ANSWER: Matched mode removes a patient's germline variants directly using the normal. Tumour-only mode can remove only variants listed in population databases (dbSNP, 1000G, ESP, ExAC), so private or rare germline variants are kept and called as somatic. Jones et al. 2015 (815 tumour-normal pairs, 15 tumour types) found that after removing common germline variants, tumour-only analysis still gave false positives making up 31% of alterations in targeted panels and 65% in exomes (about 249 of 382 candidate calls per exome were germline). The rate is higher in people of non-European ancestry (BMC Med Genomics 2017). A large virtual normal removes more than 96% of the variants a matched normal removes. So 'present in unmatched tumour, absent in matched derived sample' calls may be largely residual germline variants rather than real mutation loss. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4442685/, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12920-017-0296-8, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561496/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How does the observed log2 copy-ratio of a segment depend on tumour purity and ploidy, and is a linear regression of one sample's log2 ratios on another's adequate to remove purity differences? ANSWER: CNVkit docs state that the observed copy ratio depends on purity, ploidy and subclone size; in a pure diploid sample a one-copy gain is log2(3/2)=0.585 and a one-copy loss is -1. The standard admixture model used by ASCAT and ABSOLUTE is log2R = log2[(p*CN + 2(1-p)) / (p*ploidy + 2(1-p))]. I did not find the explicit equation in the extracted text I read; it comes from these methods as standardly given. The relation is linear in ratio space (2^log2R) but nonlinear (logarithmic) in log2 space, and it compresses losses more strongly than gains as purity falls. A linear regression of one sample's log2 ratios on another's therefore cannot fully remove a purity difference. It leaves systematic residuals at deep losses and high-level gains, which could be counted as artefactual 'changes'. The correction is to rescale in linear ratio space or to convert both samples to absolute copy number with purity and ploidy estimates (e.g. CNVkit call --purity, ASCAT, ABSOLUTE). HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383288/, https://unclineberger.org/peroulab/wp-content/uploads/sites/1008/2019/06/Aug-23-ASCAT-aCGH-VanLoo-PNAS-2010.pdf.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Do standard whole-exome capture kits cover the region just upstream of a gene's TSS? When a MAF lists both exome and whole-genome sequencing, are WGS non-coding calls normally merged into the same MAF? ANSWER: No for standard kits. Exome capture targets coding exons and leaves out non-genic control elements such as promoters. Vendors advertise TERT-promoter coverage as an extra (Agilent SureSelect V8, Nonacus cancer exome) and note that standard exomes do not cover it. Any upstream calls in exome data would be off-target reads with patchy coverage. So zero 5'Flank calls in exome samples does not mean the variants are absent. Whether WGS non-coding calls were merged into the MAF depends on the study, and the web does not settle it. Check the MAF itself: if WGS samples carry intergenic, intron or 5'Flank calls, their non-coding calls were kept. HOW SURE: high on exome coverage; low on the MAF merging question, which the web did not settle. SOURCES: https://www.genome.gov/Pages/Research/DIR/DIRNewsFeatures/Next-Gen101/Biesecker_Exome101.pdf, https://nonacus.com/germline/exome-panel/, https://www.agilent.com/about/newsroom/presrel/2021/02jun-ca21013.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In public cancer-genomics portals, how is TERT promoter mutation status usually distributed for studies that have it: as a MAF row with a 5'Flank/upstream class, as a clinical sample attribute, or as a separate table? ANSWER: In cBioPortal there are two conventions, and a separate table is not one of them. (1) MAF rows: TERT promoter variants are kept as data_mutations rows on gene TERT (Entrez 7015) with Variant_Classification 5'Flank. The cBioPortal loader's mutation filter drops 5'Flank mutations except for TERT, which is whitelisted, and sets the protein change to 'Promoter'. This is typical for targeted-panel studies whose assay covers the promoter. (2) Clinical sample attribute: TCGA whole-exome MAFs generally lack TERT promoter calls, because those came from separate targeted assays. cBioPortal datahub issue #154 states that TCGA studies including LGG/GBM did not have this data loaded. Where curators later added it (e.g. thca_tcga_pub, PR #1753, 2023), they used a 'TERT' clinical variable taken from the paper's supplementary table. For a TCGA-style GBM study, the teams should look for TERT rows with 5'Flank or 'Promoter' in data_mutations.txt and for any TERT* column in the clinical files. If neither exists, the dataset has no promoter variable. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/895, https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/issues/154, https://github.com/cBioPortal/datahub/pull/1753.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-style discrete copy-number tables from targeted clinical panels, what do the values -2, -1, 1 and 2 represent, and what thresholds are typically used to call them? ANSWER: -2 = deep (likely homozygous) deletion, -1 = shallow (likely hemizygous) loss, 0 = diploid, 1 = low-level gain, 2 = high-level amplification. With GISTIC the low-level (+/-1) threshold is static (typically 0.1 or 0.3 log2 ratio) and the high-level (+/-2) threshold is set per sample from arm-level copy number. cBioPortal stores only +/-2 as CNA events in patient views. MSK-IMPACT clinical CNA files usually contain only 0 and +/-2 (sometimes -1.5 for hemizygous): clinical calls are focal amplifications and homozygous deletions based on fold change, roughly >=2 for amplification, and shallow changes are mostly not reported. Counting only +/-2 therefore matches convention, and low-level changes cannot be assessed reliably from such tables. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/qP_OaeRdbDo, https://docs.cbioportal.org/user-guide/faq/, https://github.com/cBioPortal/cbioportal/issues/4664, https://github.com/chris-kreitzer/IMPACT_Prostate.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When comparing serial tumour samples sequenced with a targeted panel, what standard practice distinguishes truly acquired mutations from mutations present below the calling threshold in the earlier sample (for example genotyping the earlier sample at the later sample's sites)? ANSWER: The usual practice is to force-genotype ('fill out') the union of mutations called in any of a patient's samples across all of that patient's samples, at MSK with GetBaseCountsMultiSample (GBCM). A mutation is called acquired only if the earlier sample has no or negligible supporting reads at adequate depth; otherwise it is classed as shared or subclonal. MSK-IMPACT de novo calling needs about 5% VAF and at least 10 mutant reads off hotspots (about 2% at hotspots), so mutations below those levels in the earlier sample can look acquired. The pages I opened came back truncated and did not settle this; the answer rests on search snippets and domain knowledge. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-24109-5, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4940024/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808190/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How do successive versions of a widely used hybridisation-capture clinical cancer gene panel (341, 410, 468 and 505 gene versions) differ in gene content, and are earlier panels' genes strict subsets of later ones? ANSWER: For 341, 410 and 468, the panels are nested as published: all IMPACT-341 genes are in IMPACT-410 and IMPACT-468. IMPACT-410 adds 69 genes (e.g. VEGFA, ACVR1, FOXO1, CALR, H3F3A, HIST1H3 cluster, HLA-A, STAT3, ZFHX3). IMPACT-468 adds about 58 more (e.g. AGO2, CYSLTR2, DROSHA, HLA-B, PDCD1LG2, SHOC2, SPRED1, SOS1, MSH3, PPARG, TP53BP1). IMPACT-505 adds about 37 genes to 468, but I did not obtain its list from a page I read, so whether 468 is fully contained in 505 is not verified. Alterations seen only in a later sample in genes added by a later panel may reflect coverage rather than acquisition, so comparisons should be limited to genes common to both samples' panels (see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt). HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.thelancet.com/cms/10.1016/S2589-7500(21)00104-7/attachment/93631f3d-043d-42b8-b9b4-c0df6cc9a5cb/mmc1.pdf, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/25/21/6346/81935/Clinical-Genomic-Sequencing-of-Pediatric-and-Adult.

text: REPLY Q1 purity scaling: de-diluting JuP3-JP's log2 ratios with R=(2^x-(1-p))/p, JP FGA at |log2|>0.1 overtakes IDC (0.188) only at an assumed JP purity of about 0.2 (FGA 0.23), and at |log2|>0.2 or >0.3 JP stays below DCIS and IDC down to p=0.15. Bringing JP's max |seg.mean| (0.21) to DCIS's level (1.68) needs p of about 0.2 and amplifies noise segments. At 1q, the truncal gain shared by DCIS and IDC, JP is 0.007 against IDC's 0.209, which implies JP purity of only about 3% of IDC's. The label stays False.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 shared mutations: all 3 JuP3-JP mutations (PIK3CA chr3:178936082, SMG1 and CES1 on chr16) match JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC on chromosome, position and alleles, so the three lesions are clonally related. DCIS and IDC share 26 mutations, of which JP has only these 3. JP carries the truncal PIK3CA but shows about 0 at the shared arm events (1q 0.007, 6q -0.017, 8q 0.005, 16q +0.043 against negative values in DCIS and IDC). So either JP branched off before those CNAs, or its tumour fraction is very low (a few percent). Low purity cannot be ruled out, but neither reading supports a high CNA burden in JP. The label stays False and confidence goes down.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 breakpoints: I restricted to num.mark>=10, merged adjacent segments within the margin and counted breakpoints in JuP3 JP/DCIS/IDC. Margin 0.05 gives 25/31/25, 0.1 gives 23/26/17, 0.2 gives 5/12/7 and 0.3 gives 0/8/5. JP is never above DCIS. It exceeds IDC only at margin 0.1, where noise-level steps count. At margins of 0.2 and above it is lowest, which agrees with FGA. The label stays False.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 read counts: t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count and n_alt_count have 0 non-empty values for all JuP3 samples, so no VAF-based purity estimate is possible. TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS is 0.1 in JuP3-JP, 1.4 in DCIS and 1.17 in IDC. Low TMB together with near-zero CNA amplitude fits low tumour content in JP. That is a caveat on interpretation, but the observed data still show JP with fewer CNAs, not more. I reworded the reasoning to flag purity. The label stays False.

text: FINDING: No accepted classifier assigns SCLC ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3 subtypes from DNA mutation or copy-number panel data; subtypes are defined by RNA expression (NMF, Rudin 2019, Gay 2021) or IHC, and the literature states genomic profiling has not mapped to the TF-based subtypes (Chemi 2022 Nat Cancer) and genome-based stratification has failed (Sci Adv 2022). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Are SCLC molecular subtypes (ASCL1-, NEUROD1-, POU2F3-defined) ever assigned or reliably inferred from DNA-only targeted panel data (mutations or copy number) rather than from RNA or protein expression? ANSWER: No. SCLC A/N/P subtypes are defined by transcription-factor expression, measured by RNA (NMF or relative TF expression: Rudin et al. 2019 Nat Rev Cancer; Gay et al. 2021 Cancer Cell) or by IHC (Park et al. 2024 eBioMedicine, where targeted DNA sequencing was only compared across IHC-defined subtypes). QUESTION: Which ARAF missense variants, if any, are annotated as oncogenic or as MAPK-activating in curated knowledge bases (such as OncoKB or Cancer Hotspots), and what functional assays established them? ANSWER: OncoKB curates ARAF N217I as Oncogenic / Gain-of-function and ARAF G322S as Likely Oncogenic / Likely Gain-of-function. S214C was established in immortalised airway epithelial (BEAS-2B) cells by soft-agar colony formation and phospho-MEK (JCI 2014, seen only as a search snippet). So OncoKB holds prior functional evidence for exactly the two variants in the hypothesis. That evidence comes from a functional study of iCCA cell lines, not from genomic data alone. Cancer Hotspots was not checked. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://staging.oncokb.org/gene/ARAF, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/ARAF/N217I, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/ARAF/G322S.
